item.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers.

The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host.

"On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said.

The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine.

The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames.

In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload.

What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder.

It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation.

The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed.

Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online.

"Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said.

"As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026."

Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups.

"An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs."

"A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

item.title: Critical binary-parser Flaw Enables JavaScript Injection via Malicious Parser Definitions (2026)
item.description:
A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1.

"Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

"Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled."

According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation.

The parser options include -

  • length
  • lengthInBytes
  • key
  • tag
  • offset, and
  • the alias passed to namely()

"Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead."

CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters.

"[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

item.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: VMware 0-Day, Java4Shell, NGINX2Root, Ruby2Shell, and a Whole Lot of Shell Trouble (2026)
item.description:
A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open.

This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need.

The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week.

⚡ Threat of the Week

Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines.

Is Your Workforce Secured from AI Threats?

Attackers now weaponize AI to launch personalized phishing attacks faster than employees can react. Fight AI with AI, using realistic simulations to train employees to spot and stop threats. Stop phishing before it becomes a breach.

Book a Demo ➝

🔔 Top News

  • Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks.
  • Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."
  • Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue.
  • New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.
  • GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser).

🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

  • 6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers.
  • 8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts.
  • Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them.

📰 Around the Cyber World

  • Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections.
  • The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers.
  • A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India.
  • The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs.
  • Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries.
  • Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.
  • Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism.
  • Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed.
  • Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027. 
  • Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days."
  • Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both."
  • Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025.
  • Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences."
  • At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service."

Conclusion

The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done.

That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

item.title: Webworm Suspected of Modifying SoftEther VPN to Evade Detection and Hide Remote Access (2026)
item.description:
The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks.

The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence.

First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations.

One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The mutated version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026.

"The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions."

The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN."

One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity.

It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response.

The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark.

Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below -

  • Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB.
  • Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII.

What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth.

"It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools.

"We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

item.title: Hackers Exploit N-able MailAssure Flaw While AI Agents Exploit MONAI Label Zero-Day (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The critical vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.
  • CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored.

"N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity."

CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement.

The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China.

"In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step."

Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server.

"In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root."

Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network.

The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, and AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge, revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft -

  • AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization.
  • AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain.
  • AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access.

In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework.

"The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said. "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection."

According to Datadog Security Labs, ARTEX also appears under other names like ScopeWeaver, LUCK — 自主资产控制台 (LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console), and 观澜SEC渗透测试平台 (Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform).

In-the-wild activity involving ARTEX has also targeted several AWS environments with an aim to access financial data. Initial access vectors used in these attacks include compromised long-term AWS access keys and public Cognito user pools, with the latter being used to register an account, collect tokens, and enumerate AWS accounts.

"In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents," security researcher Julie Agnes Sparks said. "The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like fund, invoice, billing, and LLC."

Telemetry data gathered by Previdian from its sensors has recorded 52 HTTP requests containing explicit ARTEX markers between October 18 and November 15, 2026, from 10 source IP addresses.

"Further investigation of these sources identified 3,651 related HTTP records involving application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal and attempts to retrieve sensitive configuration data," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said.

"The most significant activity targeted Oracle WebLogic, Langflow, and Flowise, with additional payloads associated with Apache Struts, Log4j, and PHPUnit."

Interestingly, one of the IP addresses associated with ARTEX activity, 31.22.91[.]156, overlaps with the AWS-documented campaign targeting AI infrastructure, including Langflow exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2025-3248.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the latest fixes for the two flaws by November 26, 2026.

item.title: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching (2026)
item.description:
OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.

"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.

The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.

The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.

Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.

The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.

To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.

"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said. "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."

Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.

Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.

"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

This involves the following steps -

  • An agent is tasked with finding new vulnerabilities in an application, or working off external sources of new vulnerability disclosures.
  • Shirudo on the operator machine builds a security shield consisting of eBPF or application bytecode after reproducing and validating the exploit.
  • The shield is delivered as signed .bee packages via an OCI-compliant registry.
  • The Shirudo layer on each target pulls these .bee packages, validating each signature using TPMs to establish trust and safety.

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.

OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.

"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."

"Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative."

item.title: WHMCS SQL Injection Could Expose Customer Data and Admin Password Hashes without Login (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed.

The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three.

Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet.

The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline.

The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time.

Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release.

Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation.

The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says.

The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says.

It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails.

All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon.

For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to:

  1. Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu.
  2. Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache.
  3. Update to a fixed release.

The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough.

This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

item.title: Microsoft Fixes Azure API Management Classic Flaw as Actor Targets Customer Secrets (2026)
item.description:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

"An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been."

The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses.

According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected.

"On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory.

"Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include -

  • Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers
  • Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers
  • Subscription keys
  • Tokens used to call direct management APIs

As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

Cutting SOC expenses means little if slower detection increases the risk of costly incidents. For 2027, investments should be evaluated against their ability to prevent attacks from escalating into serious breaches.

item.title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity (2026)
item.description:
A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398.

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis.

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE.

What to patch

On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it.

.NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694.

Flaw Affected Fixed in
CVE-2026-87268 (VirtualBox) VirtualBox 7.2.16, Windows hosts Oracle's September update, build 7.2.18
CVE-2026-108398 (.NET Framework) .NET Framework 4 on Windows, UMCI case tested on Windows 11 S Mode October 13 update, per-version KB

Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.

item.title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap (2026)
item.description:
Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Immutability Is Not Provenance

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:

  • Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.
  • Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.
  • Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

What You'll Learn

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

  • What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create
  • How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible
  • What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't
  • Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Who Should Attend

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

item.title: Okta Links ShinyHunters-Associated Vishing Group to New INCEPTION Data Leak Site (2026)
item.description:
A threat cluster previously assessed to be affiliated with the ShinyHunters extortion crew may have rebranded and continued operations under a new name called INCEPTION, according to Okta's Threat Intelligence team.

The cluster, dubbed O-UNC-053, is characterized by the use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Okta said it's been tracking the group since March 2026.

The identity and access management provider said targets of this cluster previously had stolen data published to the ShinyHunters data leak site (DLS). However, as of November 16, 2026, a new data leak site operating under the name INCEPTION has listed the data siphoned from O-UNC-053 targets.

"While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion," Okta researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Social engineering and credential harvesting attacks mounted by O-UNC-053 have targeted a broad range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, biotechnology, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality, and legal.

Similar to O-UNC-066 and UNC6671, the newly identified cluster also relies on a phishing kit to intercept authentication flows and capture a user's credentials and MFA codes. However, the kit is not designed to bypass phishing-resistant methods like passkeys and Okta FastPass.

"While interacting with targeted users on the phone, the operators socially engineer them into sharing factors like one-time passcodes and approving push notifications," Okta said. "If successful, the operators gain access to SaaS applications and exfiltrate sensitive data, which is often used to extort targets under the threat of releasing it on a data leak site."

Domains created by the group are registered through NiceNIC, Spaceship, Tucows, and NameSilo, with the domain names using the following patterns -

  • legal-<target>[.]com
  • legaldept-<target>[.]com
  • <target>[.]legal
  • <target>-legal[.]com

The use of "legal" themes in these attacks is said to have started in October 2026, and is often registered on or within a day of a campaign starting. Prior campaign waves have employed help desk-, support-, and claims-related themes for the registered domains.

These findings also dovetail with an alert from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which has warned of widespread vishing activity using legal-themed domains that either begin with "legal-" or end with "-legal" using the ".com" top-level domain.

More than 70 such domains have been observed since October 2026, it said, adding each domain is specifically created for an intended target operating in different industries, like cryptocurrency, financial services, healthcare, high technology, and hospitality, among others.

"Registered in rapid evening batches and shielded behind Cloudflare, these web-only domains deploy a filtered kit that delivers tailored content to intended victims while routing visitors it is not configured to attack to the targeted organization's legitimate Okta or NetIQ sign-in flow," ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons said.

Some of the confirmed domains linked to the activity are listed below -

  • legal-pepsico[.]com
  • legal-paychex[.]com
  • legal-duolingo[.]com
  • activisionblizzard-legal[.]com
  • legal-westernunion[.]com
  • legal-dropbox[.]com
  • legal-indeed[.]com
  • legal-creditkarma[.]com
  • legal-amd[.]com
  • legal-grubhub[.]com
  • legal-twitch[.]tv

The crux of the campaign is to tailor the landing page to the specific identity provider of the target, while filtering unwanted visitors and forwarding them to the organization's authentication infrastructure, such as Okta.

"Throughout our tracking of O-UNC-053 between March and September 2026, we observed the names of targeted entities appear on the ShinyHunters DLS between 1 and 28 days after the phishing infrastructure was registered," Okta noted.

However, it's unclear at this stage if the published data on the INCEPTION site is authentic and whether they are running the site themselves or are collaborating with another extortion gang. The exact nature of the relationship between ShinyHunters and O-UNC-053 is also unknown.

It's worth noting that the ShinyHunters data leak site went offline in late September 2026 following the arrest of three alleged members of the group, including a Canadian co-conspirator responsible for the breach of the FBIjobs.gov portal.

There is no evidence of data from O-UNC-053 targets being published on any data leak site from early September 2026 through October and early November 2026, until listings for multiple targets appeared on the INCEPTION site last week. 

"This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors," Okta said. "Regardless of the nature of the relationship with the INCEPTION DLS, O-UNC-053 remains active in conducting vishing attacks against targets in an effort to take over accounts, steal data, and extort targets."

INCEPTION Denies ShinyHunters Link

In a post on their dark web site, INCEPTION has denied any affiliation with ShinyHunters, insisting that it operates independently with its own members and objectives. 

"We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are INCEPTION," the group said, adding "certain parties in the threat intelligence industry have been eager to give us a history we never asked for."

"We are also not copying anyone. If our methodology resembles what came before, it is because we took inspiration from operators who, whatever else may be said of them, understood that the weakest component of any secure system is a human being holding a phone. That is not theft of tradecraft. It is acknowledgment of a good idea -- the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit."

When reached for comment regarding INCEPTION's latest claims, Okta told The Hacker that its "threat intelligence advisories are built on rigorous analysis of observed threat activity and documented operational patterns," adding "our priority is to shed light on the evolution of phishing campaigns and help organizations strengthen their defenses with phishing-resistant authentication."

(The story was updated after publication to include a statement posted by INCEPTION on its dark web site and a response from Okta.)

item.title: VMware vCenter Hit by Another Critical 9.8-Rated Auth Bypass Flaw After Zero-Day Exploitation (2026)
item.description:
Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication.

The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir").

"A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today.

The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam and XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw.

Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5).

The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5).

The issues have been addressed in the following versions -

  • VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2
  • VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300
  • VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m
  • VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)
  • VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - Fixed in 5.2.5

item.title: Iran-Aligned Volant Manticore Uses IPFS-Based KuboShell Backdoor in Espionage Campaigns (2026)
item.description:
A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus.

Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025.

Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to collect email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations.

The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

"While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments."

This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives.

Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel.

This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

"This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said.

As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia.

A Windows backdoor, KuboShell uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network.

"On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained.

"KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token."

Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server.

It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process -

  • PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory
  • PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor
  • JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands

It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown.

"We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said.

The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe."

"Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention."

"If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

item.title: WordPress Blocks Six Backdoored WP Connect Plugins Before Malicious Releases Go Live (2026)
item.description:
WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account.

The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent."

The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below -

  • Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress (2.9.1 – 2.9.4)
  • WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress (1.7.4)
  • Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms (2.6.3)
  • Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable (2.5.4)
  • Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion (1.6.4)
  • Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce (1.0.2)

These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched.

"Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said.

Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval().

It can also perform the following actions -

  • Accept queued commands that run shell commands
  • Read, write, and delete arbitrary files
  • Query arbitrary database tables
  • Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes
  • Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing
  • Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code

As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal.

Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible.

"Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland said. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally."

The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors.

The site carried "thirteen separate ClickFix injections from three distinct kits [LOM, ErrTraffic, and Macfinger], alongside seven further malicious loaders," it said. "Several of the injections attempt to remove each other's code and overlays, and one injection disables another through a JavaScript naming collision. Five of the thirteen injections resolve their next-stage infrastructure from Polygon smart contracts, a technique known as EtherHiding."
